conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** 
Yes, heavy current and former smokers are significantly less likely to die of lung cancer if they undergo regular screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT).

**Key Evidence:**

* **The National Lung Screening Trial (NLST):** A randomized trial of over 53,000 high-risk current and former heavy smokers demonstrated a ~20% reduction in lung cancer mortality among participants who received annual LDCT screenings compared to those receiving standard chest X-rays.
* **The NELSON Trial:** A large European randomized controlled trial of heavy smokers similarly demonstrated that volume-based LDCT screening significantly reduces lung cancer deaths compared to no screening.
* **Systematic Reviews and Clinical Guidelines:** Comprehensive evidence syntheses—including systematic reviews supporting the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommendations—confirm that annual LDCT screening effectively detects early-stage lung cancer and lowers disease-specific mortality in adults at high risk due to age and cumulative smoking exposure (e.g., 20 or more pack-years). Systematic reviews note a statistically significant reduction in lung cancer mortality, although a statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality is generally not observed.

**Sources:**
* https://www.cancer.gov/types/lung/research/nlst
* https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793
* https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11718421/
* https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2777244
